item.title: Xinhua Commentary: China, ASEAN have every reason to deepen cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16
MANILA, Nov. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese proverb "a close neighbor is better than a distant relative" also applies to the relations between China and ASEAN, who share an enduring bond and see their cooperation bring tangible benefits to people across the region. At a time of growing global uncertainties, the two sides have every reason to deepen their partnership, focus on shared interests and keep their cooperation moving forward. The strength of China-ASEAN relations lies in their shared interests and the practical benefits they deliver. This partnership is too important to be distracted by occasional differences, political rhetoric or external attempts to sow discord. There is a clear reason for keeping this partnership on track: its benefits are real and far-reaching. China has remained ASEAN's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has been China's biggest trading partner for six successive years. This year also marks the fifth anniversary of the establishment of the China-ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and the 35th anniversary of China-ASEAN dialogue relations, making it an important milestone for taking stock of achievements and charting the way forward. China has consistently demonstrated its commitment to building a closer China-ASEAN community with a shared future, backing its pledges with concrete actions. With China's participation, the China-Laos Railway has turned Laos from a landlocked to a land-linked nation. Under the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative, the Sihanoukville Special Economic Zone has made Cambodia a rising manufacturing and export hub. Across Southeast Asia, infrastructure connectivity, industrial cooperation and people-to-people exchanges are creating opportunities that extend well beyond national borders. Cooperation is also expanding into emerging fields. The implementation of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol and closer coordination with the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement will open new avenues for trade and investment. In electric vehicles, digital technologies, renewable energy and green agriculture, Chinese companies are increasingly working with ASEAN partners to develop solutions tailored to regional needs. Such cooperation is particularly valuable as ASEAN countries seek to upgrade their industries, strengthen economic resilience and move up global value chains. By combining China's industrial strengths, technological capabilities and vast market with ASEAN's dynamic economies and development potential, both sides can create more opportunities for businesses, especially micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. China's commitment to deeper cooperation with ASEAN also goes beyond the economic arena. It firmly supports ASEAN centrality and ASEAN-led regional mechanisms, and stands ready to work with regional countries to build a peaceful, stable and inclusive regional community. This year marks the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia. China was the first major country to accede to the treaty, demonstrating its support for ASEAN's principles. The development of China-ASEAN relations has never been without challenges. Differences over certain issues, including those concerning the South China Sea, should be addressed through dialogue and consultation in a constructive manner. The South China Sea, meanwhile, should remain a sea of peace, friendship and cooperation. China and ASEAN members have a common interest in maintaining stability, promoting practical maritime cooperation and ensuring the safety of shipping and trade. Differences should be properly handled through dialogue and consultation, while efforts to advance cooperation in areas such as environmental protection, marine research and sustainable development deserve greater attention. As China and ASEAN look to the future, their shared interests and common aspirations provide a strong foundation for closer cooperation. By staying committed to good-neighborliness, mutual benefit and dialogue, both sides can further strengthen their partnership, deliver greater benefits to their peoples and contribute more to peace, stability and prosperity in the region.■

item.title: Golden pomelo industry sweetens life in south China village
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
GUANGZHOU, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- In early November, south China's Guangdong Province is still warm and lush, with harvest activity in full swing as terraced pomelo orchards in the village of Nanfu in the city of Meizhou bear heavy golden fruit, while growers weave among the trees picking and sorting. Meizhou is China's second-largest pomelo-producing region and the largest in Guangdong, and is known as the "hometown of the Chinese golden pomelo." One in every five pomelos sold in China comes from Meizhou. In 2026, the city's planting area is expected to reach 670,000 mu (around 44,700 hectares), with output exceeding 1.3 million tonnes and full-industry-chain output value approaching 9 billion yuan (about 1.34 billion U.S. dollars). The golden pomelo is becoming a pillar of income growth for local farmers. COOPERATIVES HELP GROWERS SELL SMARTER Meizhou locals have a long tradition of growing pomelos, which are seen as auspicious in local culture and a signature fruit served to guests in autumn and winter. In the past, many growers planted on a small scale and sold alone, often struggling to get good prices for quality fruit or to secure stable buyers. In recent years, local authorities have built platforms and mechanisms to support the entire chain from planting to sales, promoting collective development of the pomelo industry. Yanyang Township in Meixian District of Meizhou is one of the core producing areas, featuring more than 30,000 mu of orchards, output value of nearly 400 million yuan and over 7,000 growers. Nanfu, notably, has set up a pomelo cooperative, with more than 90 percent of growers joining. The cooperative makes bulk purchases of agricultural inputs, organizes training, standardizes orchard management and coordinates sales. Nanfu's pomelo output value now exceeds 57.5 million yuan, with per capita annual income up by 28,800 yuan and pomelos accounting for more than 80 percent of growers' total income. "We used to figure out farming by ourselves, and when selling, we just waited for wholesalers to come and the prices were low. Now experts teach us techniques hands-on and help us find buyers," said Li Yongsheng, head of the Meixian golden pomelo association. Taoyao Township in Meixian runs courses timed to the farming calendar, including a three-day livestreaming workshop ahead of the pomelo season. "My first livestream sold 12 orders in an hour and a half, and 12 more the next day. Now I stream every day, orders keep growing, and I've built up a group of repeat customers," said a trainee named Zhang Xia. E-commerce is cutting out intermediaries and leaving more profit with growers. E-commerce operator Chen Zengli said he and his wife handle sales themselves and have sold over 100,000 jin (roughly 50 tonnes) more pomelos this year than last year. Meizhou has also launched a pomelo tree adoption program, opening 500 trees at 10 premium orchards for adoption. "Adoption is essentially presale. It brings consumers and orchards closer, enhances the experience, locks in sales in advance, and promotes integrated rural tourism," said Yang Jingliang, chairman of Guangdong Runtu Ecological Agriculture Co., Ltd. The industry is attracting growing numbers of young people back to their hometowns. Lin Lyu, a third-generation pomelo grower, has taken over the family orchards and moved to large-scale and standardized operations. "We have 1,700 mu of standard orchards and annual sales of 30 million jin (approximately 15,000 tonnes). We sell through wholesale, e-commerce and exports simultaneously, and many customers in Europe and Australia specifically seek out Meizhou pomelos," he said. TECHNOLOGY BOOSTS QUALITY, EFFICIENCY "I grow more than 400 pomelo trees, and output is on par with last year. The biggest surprise this year is the sweetness. Following the agricultural research institute's guidance, we spread quicklime in the orchards to reduce acidity and increase sugar content," said grower Huang Yuliang from Nanfu. Modern equipment is also boosting quality and efficiency. Hillside rail transporters now move over 350 kg of fruit per trip, and drones carry fruit baskets in the event of steep terrain. Integrated water and fertilizer systems and IoT monitoring devices, meanwhile, enable growers to irrigate and fertilize remotely via their phones. In 2025, the orchard managed by Huang Yuji in Nanfu saw output rise by about 20 percent. "We used to fertilize by feel. Now we go by data, fertilizer costs are down 15 percent, and the sugar content is more stable," he said. Drones have become common in Meizhou's mountain orchards. "Spraying an orchard that would take seven or eight people a week to do can be done by two drones in two nights, and pesticide use has dropped by 30 percent," Yang said. Agricultural technicians are stationed in the fields year-round. The agricultural research institute of Meixian has developed local management plans covering soil improvement, pruning and fruit thinning, and a special harvesting technique to reduce bruising and extend shelf life. "Only when fruit quality improves, can everyone sell in volume and at good prices," said Zhong Yonghui, head of the institute. MORE THAN JUST A POMELO A golden pomelo is valuable from skin to pulp. At the Nanfu golden pomelo base, shelves are lined with processed products such as peel candy, juice, beer and blossom tea. Local businesses are turning a single-season fruit into a diverse product range. "We have developed 40 products so far, extending the sales cycle and raising added value," Li said. Meixian has cultivated six deep-processing companies making products including pomelo tea, wine and naringin. "Fresh fruit is only available in autumn, but processed products sell year-round, making the industry more resilient," said Zhang Weisi, deputy general manager of a local company. Longer supply chains mean more jobs. Villagers find work nearby in orchard management, processing, warehousing and food services. Yang Youyuan earns a steady 5,000 yuan a month as a chef at a pomelo-themed farm restaurant. "I can care for my family here and still earn money," he said. Yanyang Township has developed picking, sightseeing and homestay businesses, attracting tourists year-round. "More self-driving tourists and tour groups come, and they stay to eat and lodge, diversifying villagers' income," said Gu Haihui of the town's economic development office. Meizhou now has 120 pomelo processing companies, shifting from selling fresh fruit to selling products. Exports of the fruit reached 2,605.86 tonnes in 2025, surging 69.1 percent year on year, while reaching more than 20 countries and regions. Meizhou has issued a three-year action plan (2026-2028) focusing on quality, brands, supply chain and incomes, aiming to push the industry's output value past 10 billion yuan and make the golden pomelo a true "golden tree." ■

item.title: Symposium honors Edgar Snow's legacy as bridge builder between China, U.S.
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
by Xinhua writers Shi Chun, Xu Jing and Xie E NEW YORK, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Scholars and representatives from China and the United States gathered in New York on Saturday for a symposium honoring Edgar Snow, the American journalist whose pioneering reporting helped introduce the Chinese revolution in the 1930s to the world and whose legacy continues to inspire efforts to foster mutual understanding between the two countries. The symposium, themed "The Bridge Builder: Remembering Edgar Snow's Journey 90 Years Ago," brought together nearly 100 participants, including Snow's family members, representatives of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation (USA), and Chinese and U.S. scholars on Snow studies. In 1936, at the age of 31, Snow broke through blockades and ventured deep into China's impoverished northwest to interview the Red Army. His reporting resulted in the groundbreaking book "Red Star Over China." After the founding of the People's Republic of China, he made three reporting trips to the country, opening a new window on "Red China" to the international community. At Saturday's symposium, speakers shared their reflections on Snow's historical contributions and contemporary influences, highlighting the enduring relevance of his efforts to bridge cultural divides and help the world gain a better understanding of China. President of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation Sidne Ward recalled a study tour this summer with Snow's relatives, international representatives and scholars retracing part of Snow's 1936 interview journey in Shaanxi and Ningxia. "It makes me feel more connected to him and to his experiences 90 years ago," she said. For Nancy Hill, president emeritus of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation, Snow has many different legacies as a premier journalist and a bridge builder. "He saw the plight of the Chinese people and cared. And he reported that story with his head but also with his heart. I think that's a really beautiful lesson that people can learn from," Hill said. Sun Hua, director of the China Center for Edgar Snow Studies at Peking University, viewed the pursuit of truth, respect for other cultures and a spirit of dedication as Snow's most precious spiritual legacy. "The reason 'Red Star Over China' has remained enduringly significant for 90 years lies in its authenticity and its unvarnished, first-hand source material. That is truly unparalleled. To this day, it remains one of the most authoritative works on the early history of the CPC," Sun said. ■

item.title: 10 years on, world's first Luban Workshop helps create brighter future for Thai youth
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
AYUTTHAYA, Thailand, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- In a classroom at Ayutthaya Technical College, home to the world's first Luban Workshop jointly established by China and Thailand, several humanoid desktop robots rhythmically waved their arms and stepped to the music as Surapat Pimrat skillfully operated them. "I named one of the robots Nam Khing because it keeps me company like a best friend," said Surapat, a third-year student pursuing Vocational Certification in mechatronics and robotics at the workshop. He added that his sister, a workshop graduate now working at Haier Thailand, inspired him to enroll. Surapat's next plan is to pursue an opportunity to deepen his expertise in China, following his sister's example: she strengthened her professional expertise and improved her Chinese-language proficiency, paving the way for her promotion to team leader. Their experiences are shared by thousands of other Thai students who have benefited from the Luban Workshop. Named after an ancient Chinese craftsman, the workshop embodies China's tradition of craftsmanship and innovation while equipping Thai youth with practical skills. In March 2016, Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College in China and Ayutthaya Technical College jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop in Thailand. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system. Recalling the workshop's early days, Jarun Youbrum, then director of Ayutthaya Technical College who was involved throughout its establishment, expressed deep appreciation for the Chinese instructors. "To help assemble and commission the equipment, they would sometimes work until two in the morning," Jarun said. "Their dedication is truly moving." Following three phases of development, the workshop's instructional space has expanded 10 folds to 2,000 square meters, with 15 teaching and practice areas established. According to Pakorn Muangsuk, head of the college's Mechatronics and Robotics department, Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College has regularly sent instructors to Thailand to train students. Ayutthaya Technical College has also dispatched its faculty to China to learn equipment operation and teaching methods. Pakorn's department adopted the EPIP (Engineering Practice Innovation Project) teaching model, which helps students build professional knowledge and practical skills through real-world engineering projects and targeted problem-solving. One valuable opportunity offered by the workshop is further training in Tianjin. Teerapat Sudso, an Internet of Things (IoT) major who enrolled in 2018, was selected to study there for over a year. Teerapat has now been working for over three years as an assistant engineer at the Thai subsidiary of Zhongji Innolight, a leading Chinese manufacturer of high-speed optical modules. He mentors both Chinese and Thai apprentices. Teerapat said the knowledge and skills he acquired at the workshop laid the foundation for his current role, and he still uses Chinese at work every day. "Graduates from our college possess both professional skills and the ability to communicate in Chinese, which gives them a distinct advantage when seeking employment," said Pakorn. He added that as Chinese-funded enterprises continue to establish factories and begin production in Ayutthaya's industrial parks, demand for frontline workers is steadily growing. Statistics from Ayutthaya Technical College show that over the past decade, Luban Workshop has cultivated more than 2,600 local students pursuing academic degrees and sent over 500 students to China for further study. Meanwhile, the Chinese and Thai colleges have jointly trained nearly 100,000 people through their partnership. A new milestone was reached in September, when Ayutthaya Technical College inaugurated the world's first EPIP Center, jointly established with Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College. The center features practical training modules in artificial intelligence, IoT, intelligent manufacturing, and other fields. "Luban Workshop has established a cooperation network spanning multiple vocational colleges, providing students from these institutions with opportunities to study in China," said Chaowarit Umboon, deputy director of Ayutthaya Technical College. Looking ahead, Chaowarit hopes to see more branch centers established across northern, southern, and northeastern Thailand, making it easier for students in these regions to pursue further studies and receive practical training. ■

item.title: Documentary | Shenzhen Through Our Eyes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15
Openness. Innovation. Cooperation. APEC 2026's priorities are also woven into the story of its host city, Shenzhen. From a border town to a global metropolis in less than half a century, Shenzhen offers a window into Chinese modernization. Ahead of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, Xinhua's Miao Xiaojuan invites the people who call Shenzhen home to spell out what makes their city special.
